stem: Four of the following five numbers share a common mathematical property. Which one does NOT belong to the group? 8, 27, 64, 100, 125

per_option_rationale.rationale: 8 = 2^3 is a perfect cube. A student might flag 8 as odd because it is the smallest, but the shared property is perfect cubes, not magnitude.
27 = 3^3 is a perfect cube. A student might confuse the grouping property with perfect squares - while 27 is not a perfect square, that is not the relevant property here.
8=2^3, 27=3^3, 64=4^3, 125=5^3 are all perfect cubes. 100=10^2 is a perfect square but not a perfect cube (cube root of 100 is approximately 4.64, not an integer).

125 = 5^3 is a perfect cube. A student who misidentifies the series as consecutive even-base cubes (2,4,6,...) might flag 125 (5^3), but 5 is not even while 2,4 are - the correct grouping is all perfect cubes.

explanation: 8=2^3, 27=3^3, 64=4^3, 125=5^3 - all are perfect cubes. 100=10^2 is a perfect square but has no integer cube root (since 4^3=64 and 5^3=125), so it is the odd one out.

explanation_sections.punchline: The shared property is perfect cube, not perfect square - 100 is a well-known perfect square that is placed as a trap.
explanation_sections.approach: Deductive trace: test each number for the most prominent grouping. Check cube roots: cbrt(8)=2, cbrt(27)=3, cbrt(64)=4, cbrt(125)=5 - all integers. cbrt(100)=4.64 - not an integer. Setup decision: recognise cube vs square as the relevant property.
explanation_sections.lesson: When you spot a mix of powers, test both perfect-square and perfect-cube hypotheses; choose the one that fits four of the five members.
explanation_sections.timing: 50-60 seconds. The trap is 100 being a well-known perfect square (10^2), which tempts misidentification of the grouping property as squares.
